step1_summary: Chief complaint: New-onset dry, itchy, red skin on hands and arms for a few days.

Symptoms: Started a few days ago, mainly hands and arms, pruritic and dry with redness; no fever, no systemic symptoms, no obvious cracking or spots; onset reported after swimming; coconut butter used without benefit; patient reports increased stress and fatigue.
Past medical history: Otherwise well; no prior skin problems (patient denies previous eczema/dermatitis).
Medications/allergies: Taking Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive). No other regular meds. No known drug allergies; reports possible lactose intolerance.

Family/social history: Father with asthma, mother with hayfever (family history of atopy). Works as a primary school teacher (possible increased handwashing/irritant exposure). Lives alone, non-smoker, minimal alcohol, no recreational drugs.

Vitals/exam findings: No vitals or physical exam details recorded beyond patient description of red, dry, itchy skin on hands/arms. Clinician suspected dermatitis and recommended topical steroid, emollients, and oral antihistamines.

V: Allergic urticaria/vasodilation: Histamine-mediated skin reaction can present with pruritus and redness; stress or exposures (swimming chemicals) can trigger. (Less likely given persistent localized dry rash rather than transient wheals.)
I: Irritant contact dermatitis (chemical/soap exposure): Onset after swimming and occupation with frequent hand exposure (teacher) supports irritant dermatitis from chlorine, pool chemicals, detergents, or handwashing.
Allergic contact dermatitis: Delayed-type hypersensitivity to an agent (eg, pool additives, topical coconut product, soap, latex) producing localized pruritic red dermatitis after exposure.
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / chronic eczema-mimic: Chronic, persistent eczema-like patches can rarely represent neoplastic processes (very unlikely with acute onset and short duration).
D: Xerosis (environmental dry skin): Seasonal/weather-related dry skin causing generalized dryness/pruritus; patient suggested "weather" as possible cause.
I2: Irritant or allergic reaction to topical product (coconut butter): New topical use temporally related to symptoms and could worsen or cause contact dermatitis.
Drug-related rash from oral contraceptive (rare): Possible but unlikely given localized distribution and timing.
C: Atopic diathesis (genetic predisposition to eczema): Family history of atopy (asthma, hayfever) increases risk of atopic dermatitis presenting with pruritic eczematous lesions.
A: Atopic dermatitis flare (immune-mediated eczema): Pruritic, red, dry skin consistent with eczematous inflammation; stress is a known trigger.
Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity): See I category but also fits allergic/immune mechanism.
T: Irritant dermatitis from repeated friction/handwashing at work: Occupational trauma to skin barrier (teachers wash hands often) leading to localized dryness and eczema.
E: Hypothyroidism-related dry skin: Can cause generalized dryness and pruritus but would not typically present acutely or be so localized; low likelihood.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset of dry, itchy, red hands/arms after swimming and working as a teacher (probable frequent handwashing/ exposure to detergents); localized distribution and absence of systemic signs are typical for irritant contact dermatitis.
supporting_evidence: Symptoms began a few days ago after swimming (temporal relationship to exposure).
Distribution on hands and arms (common sites for irritant contact dermatitis).
Occupation (teacher) implies frequent handwashing/contact with cleaning agents that damage skin barrier.
No systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) to suggest infection.
opposing_evidence: Patient reports no obvious cracked or weeping skin (although early irritant dermatitis can be just dry/red).
No documented examination findings (physician did not describe classic fissures or scaling).

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis (delayed hypersensitivity to pool chemicals, topical coconut product, soap, or other exposure)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Onset after swimming and recent application of a new topical (coconut butter) could reflect a delayed allergic contact reaction; pruritic, localized rash fits allergic dermatitis.
supporting_evidence: Temporal association with swimming and with use of coconut butter.
Pruritus and redness localized to exposed areas (hands/arms) are consistent with contact allergy.
Family history of atopy increases susceptibility to allergic skin disease.
opposing_evidence: No prior history of allergic dermatitis to suggest sensitization, though sensitization can be new.
Coconut product could also simply irritate rather than cause allergic reaction; no mention of vesicles, intense swelling, or spread that commonly occurs in severe allergic contact dermatitis.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Atopic diathesis suggested by family history (asthma, hayfever); stress is a known precipitant and lesions can be pruritic and eczematous on the hands/arms. Adult-onset eczema is possible.
supporting_evidence: Family history of atopy (father asthma, mother hayfever).
Patient reports recent stress and fatigue which can precipitate an atopic flare.
Presentation of dry, itchy, red skin fits eczema phenotype.
opposing_evidence: Patient denies prior personal history of eczema (no childhood atopy reported).
Acute temporal relationship to swimming and topical application points more toward contact/irritant cause than classic chronic atopic pattern.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Irritant or allergic reaction to topical coconut product
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: New topical applied and not helpful; coconut oil can rarely cause contact allergy or exacerbate barrier disruption causing irritation, but timing suggests symptoms began after swimming and coconut butter was used subsequently.
supporting_evidence: Patient used coconut butter for a few days and symptoms persisted/worsened.
Topical products are common culprits in contact dermatitis.
opposing_evidence: Symptoms reportedly started after swimming (before/around the time coconut product used) making it less clearly primary cause.
No reported immediate burning/stinging after application to suggest irritant reaction.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Fungal or bacterial infections can cause localized rash, but acute diffuse dry itchy redness without scaling, focal cellulitic signs, systemic symptoms, or chronicity makes these less likely.
supporting_evidence: Localized hand involvement could be consistent with tinea manuum or localized infection in some cases.
opposing_evidence: No fever, systemic features, or pustules/clear scaling described.
Short duration (few days) and clear temporal association with exposure (swimming/possible irritant) favor contact dermatitis.
